C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on combining flatness and worst-group optimization while limiting the average-performance tradeoff. v2 redefines the central contribution as sufficient invariant learning, claims a connection between common flat minima and learning diverse invariant features, and introduces ASGDRO and H-CMNIST as contributions supporting that claim. This changes the scientific scope of the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds the failure-mode argument that successfully learned invariant cues can disappear at test time, and interprets GDRO's limitations as learning only a subset of available invariant features. Sections 3.2–3.3 also introduce scale-symmetry qualifications and explain how group-specific perturbations could distort sharpness comparisons and group weights. These substantially expand the earlier flatness and average-versus-worst-group interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendices A, B, and D substantially expand reproducibility information: dataset construction, model selection, architectures, optimizers, batch sizes, epochs, search ranges, group-adjustment parameters, and second-step gradient clipping. v2 also identifies reused LISA, JTT, SAM, and DPLCLIP code resources. These are substantial documentation additions beyond v1's brief settings and references, although v1's explicit Power-method description for Hessian estimation disappears.

E1.justification: v2 adds H-CMNIST with missing-invariant-feature tests, CelebA, CivilComments toxicity classification, Multi-NLI inference, and evaluations on Camelyon17, RxRx1, FMoW, Amazon, and MetaShift. Waterbirds and four visual DomainBed datasets remain. RotatedMNIST disappears; ColoredMNIST remains under a subpopulation-shift setup rather than the earlier DomainBed evaluation.

E2.justification: The Waterbirds comparison replaces SAM with ASAM and adds IRM, IB-IRM, V-REx, CORAL, DomainMix, Fish, and LISA to the earlier ERM/GDRO comparison. DomainBed replaces the earlier algorithm panel with DPLCLIP, DPLCLIP+GDRO, and multiple backbone comparisons. Appendix C also includes LISA in the new Grad-CAM comparisons.

E3.justification: Waterbirds replaces the stated fixed rho=0.1 and method-specific L2 penalties with hyperparameter searches, including rho in {0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8}. DomainBed moves to DPLCLIP-based training and increases the reported hyperparameter-search budget from five trials to twenty. Appendix D adds test-domain validation, explicitly labeled oracle selection, alongside the retained training-domain selection approach.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled H-CMNIST tests removing color and spurious box-position cues, a two-feature Gaussian toy analysis, and Grad-CAM studies on Waterbirds and CelebA, including Appendix C. Waterbirds Hessian analysis is revised and supplemented by a CelebA group-wise Hessian comparison. v1's empirical parameter-perturbation loss curves are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports five random seeds for Waterbirds; v2 Appendix A.6 reports three for its subpopulation experiments. The Waterbirds display loses the earlier per-group uncertainty values and reports only summary accuracies. DomainBed retains three-seed reporting and plus/minus entries, but v2 no longer explicitly identifies those entries as standard errors, as v1 did.

E6.justification: Waterbirds results are replaced: v1 Table 1 reports worst-group accuracies of 87.2% for SGDRO and 86.5% for GDRO; v2 Table 2 reports 91.0% for ASGDRO and 90.6% for GDRO. Changed methods and tuning prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains. v2 also adds extensive H-CMNIST, real-world, qualitative, and domain-specific results and replaces the earlier DomainBed and Hessian entries. New oracle results include a TerraIncognita exception: DPLCLIP+ASGDRO scores 52.2%, below DPLCLIP's 52.6%.

M1.justification: v1's SGDRO uses SAM's normalized overall-loss gradient for perturbation. v2's ASGDRO introduces ASAM's element-wise or filter-wise normalization operator, changing the perturbation geometry and training updates in Equation 2 and Algorithm 1. The shared perturbation and multiplicative group-weight updates are retained, but the adaptive component is an actual procedural change.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Sharpness-aware Minimization for Worst Case Optimization' to 'Sufficient Invariant Learning for Distribution Shift.' The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Methodology and results are reorganized around SIL, with separate subpopulation, domain-shift, real-world, and interpretability sections and new appendices organizing experimental details and extended results.

P2.justification: v1's trajectory and empirical loss-surface displays are removed. v2 adds SIL and dataset illustrations, Gaussian toy plots, benchmark and Hessian bar charts, and extensive Grad-CAM grids. Waterbirds accuracy and Hessian tables change column structure, DomainBed comparisons are redesigned, and Appendix D adds domain-specific and oracle tables. Several figures and tables also adopt side-by-side placement.

R1.justification: v2 substantially redirects research positioning toward invariant-feature learning and general distribution shifts. It adds discussions and citations concerning SWAD, flatness-aware domain generalization, DPLCLIP, LISA, and feature learning under spurious correlations, while removing several classical DRO and SAM-efficiency references. Already-cited ASAM becomes central, and the novelty argument shifts toward sufficient invariant learning while acknowledging prior flatness-based domain-generalization research.

T1.justification: v1 Section 3.1's small-rho Taylor expansion and gradient-curvature argument are removed. v2 Section 3.1 instead constructs Gaussian group-loss functions with two feature-associated parameters, explicit covariance choices, equal-group-size assumptions, and objective comparisons under different sharpness conditions. This substantially changes the mathematical justification; the new analysis is an illustrative construction with explicit assumptions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support and reproducibility. Where v1 mainly offers Waterbirds and aggregate DomainBed evidence, v2 directly tests missing-invariant-cue failure through H-CMNIST, adds feature visualizations and broader original evaluations, and documents training and model-selection procedures in Appendices A, B, and D. Reduced Waterbirds uncertainty reporting and the absence of a general proof for the SIL guarantees remain weaknesses, but the targeted diagnostic evidence and substantially improved experimental documentation provide a clear net quality gain.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and substantial revision, both PDFs describe the same research lineage, retaining the shared-perturbation group-robust optimization framework. Text, equations, tables, and figures are readable throughout. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes readable Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v2 reports original H-CMNIST experiments, ASGDRO evaluations across multiple distribution-shift benchmarks, and Grad-CAM and Hessian analyses. Appendix D also reports domain-specific and oracle-selection results.

before.justification: v1 reports original SGDRO experiments on Waterbirds and DomainBed, together with Hessian eigenvalues and empirical loss-surface analyses. These qualify independently of the baseline results attributed to earlier work.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, and contributions expand from calibrated 4p3v solutions to claimed first efficient solutions for the previously unsolved 4p3vf problem. v2 presents broader M- and L-based solver families and removes v1's concluding suggestion that 4p3v might have limited practical relevance. The general virtual-correspondence framework claim is retained.

C2.justification: v1 mainly anticipates an advantage under heavy outlier contamination; v2 interprets controlled iteration-based experiments as supporting that use case while retaining a preference for 5pt+P3P with fewer outliers and ample computation. New discussion addresses 6pt degeneracies, using a network trained for the calibrated problem, geometry-dependent δ selection, and the distinction between correspondence-error bounds and potentially large pose errors.

D1.justification: v2 documents the replacement network's layer widths, pooling, activations, and training recipe, plus δ choices and KITTI triplet construction. It newly specifies unbatched CPU inference and changes the reported CPU from i9-10900K to i9-10900X. Public release remains prospective; v2 promises solver source code, whereas v1 also explicitly promised the network and training data.

E1.justification: v2 adds the unknown-shared-focal-length task and KITTI driving imagery, plus controlled high-outlier scenarios on PhotoTourism. The original Cambridge Landmarks, ETH3D, and PhotoTourism coverage remains, including the supplementary two-view task.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates new consecutive 6pt, joint 6pt, 6pt+P3P, and 4p3vf(O) comparators for partially calibrated cameras (Table 2). In the retained two-view comparison, v1 Table 3's learned 4p(L) method is replaced by 4p(M±δ) in v2 Table 6. The original calibrated baseline families remain.

E3.justification: Reported training changes from 1,500 to 30 epochs and batches of 2,048 to 1,024. Synthetic scene size changes from 100×100×100 with camera distances 130–150 to 10×10×10 with distances 20–50; the 1M instances and 70/30 split remain. New protocols include controlled inlier ratios and iteration budgets, while KITTI uses AUC thresholds of 1°, 2.5°, 5°, and 10°.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled outlier robustness tests at inlier ratios 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4, and δ sensitivity sweeps (Figures 3 and 8–10; Tables 4–5). Noise tests extend to the new solver variants and partially calibrated task. Some separate second-pair error panels from v1 disappear, while combined pose and first-pair diagnostics remain.

E5.justification: Both versions use instance-level median and quartile boxplots with the same whisker convention, alongside average timings. Neither reports training seeds, uncertainty across repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Additional experimental instances and result rows do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Many retained Table 1 entries change: Sacre Coeur AUC@5° for 4p3v(L) changes from 47.14 to 42.84, and for 4p3v(O) from 47.83 to 50.18. v2 adds KITTI, outlier, and δ-sweep results and replaces the two-view learned result. The changed learned model and timing hardware limit direct cross-version performance comparisons.

M1.justification: v2 replaces the Set Transformer with a shared-MLP/max-pooling network, changes its input from 5×6 to 4×6, revises normalization, and replaces the symmetric epipolar loss with a Sampson loss for a predicted shift. It also adds perturbation variants and 4p3vf solvers that generate two virtual correspondences and use 6pt+P3P for unknown shared focal length.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, discussion, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Method exposition is reorganized into calibrated and partially calibrated cases, with mean-based methods presented before learned methods. General-framework discussion and detailed oracle/noise material move into a substantially reorganized, numbered supplement with a future-work section.

P2.justification: v2 adds outlier plots, a geometric proof illustration, a network architecture diagram, and KITTI and sensitivity tables. Calibrated solver timings move from a separate table into Table 1's final column. Noise figures are reorganized in the supplement with expanded legends and partially calibrated panels; the retained two-view table is renumbered and revised.

R1.justification: v2 positions the work as addressing a previously unsolved shared-focal-length problem, extending its novelty beyond competing calibrated solvers. It adds discussion of Ding et al.'s generalized three-view homotopy work and references supporting NeFSAC-style architecture, KITTI, and additional solver components. The established homotopy-continuation and epipole-search comparisons remain central.

T1.justification: v2 Section 8 adds Lemma 1 and a geometric proof of the triangle-intersection property stated informally in v1 Section 3.3, supporting the existing virtual-correspondence distance bound. Section 3 also extends the degrees-of-freedom argument to unknown shared focal length. General pose-error propagation bounds remain unestablished.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: controlled outlier tests replace v1's speculation about practical usefulness with iteration-based evidence, while KITTI evaluations and δ sweeps test the framework's extension and design choices. The proof and implementation details strengthen its rationale and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed learned two-view comparison and lower reported AUC of the revised learned solver; hardware changes still limit cross-version timing conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same virtual-correspondence research, although v2 extends it to partially calibrated cameras. All pages, including equations, figures, tables, and supplementary material, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original calibrated and partially calibrated pose evaluations, including PhotoTourism and KITTI results, controlled outlier tests, and parameter sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, noise tests, PhotoTourism evaluations on 10,000 image triplets, and supplementary two-view results on 9,900 image pairs.

C1.justification: v2 presents mean-point and learned solvers as two principal contributions and describes 4p3vf as previously unsolved. v3 centers refined mean-point solvers, characterizes learning results as preliminary with negligible gains after refinement, and positions its focal-length solutions as efficient alternatives to existing homotopy methods.

C2.justification: v3 adds concrete explanations of low-overlap failures, small-triangle instability, and why an additional real correspondence can make 5pt+P3P more robust. It explains filtering's accuracy cost and refinement's reduction of the learning advantage. Its appendix attributes the revised oracle ranking to RANSAC termination behavior, although the main text retains the earlier contrary statement.

D1.justification: v3 documents a substantially revised experimental recipe, including a 2,048-feature cap, Cambridge resizing to 800 pixels, triplet eligibility requirements, PoseLib's 0.9999 stopping confidence, and hardware for runtime comparisons. v2's explicit C++/Eigen and default HC-implementation disclosures are omitted. The detailed network training recipe remains, and both versions still promise a future code release.

E1.justification: v3 expands PhotoTourism evaluation beyond v2's two principal scenes and expands Cambridge Landmarks from the Shop Facade correspondence analysis to five-scene calibrated and shared-focal-length evaluation. KITTI driving-scene evaluation disappears. Synthetic training and ETH3D noise experiments remain; two-view estimation was already evaluated in v2.

E2.justification: v2's real-data comparisons include consecutive and joint 5pt/6pt estimation baselines, which v3 omits from the corresponding real-data comparisons. The joint 5PC comparator survives in the noise experiments. HC, 5pt/6pt+P3P, and oracle families remain. Newly cited GPU homotopy methods are explicitly not evaluated.

E3.justification: Real-data matching changes from RootSIFT with nearest-neighbor matching to SuperPoint/LightGlue, and evaluation adds PoseLib alongside GC-RANSAC. v3 selects δ=0.04 and refinement iterations using held-out St. Peter's Square, replacing v2's reported 0.15/0.1 shifts. It adds runtime-based evaluation and an all-camera-pairs error metric. Calibrated-solver timing sample counts change from 1,000 to over 10,000 instances, without establishing that those timings were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds refinement/filtering comparisons, an LM-iteration ablation, alternative-metric validation, and raw 4pt(M)-versus-5pt pose-accuracy analysis. Mean-point analysis now examines pose errors and recovered inliers as well as epipolar error. The δ and outlier studies are substantially revised, including runtime-based robustness comparisons; the earlier noise experiments remain.

E5.justification: v3 Table 1 newly reports ± quantities alongside mean errors and adds 20th-percentile summaries. The meaning of the ± quantities is not explicitly defined. Existing noise boxplots and their quantile conventions remain, and neither version documents seed-based confidence intervals or repeated-run significance testing.

E6.justification: Many results are added or replaced. v2 Table 2 reports KITTI AUC@5 of 72.05 for 4p3vf(M±0.15) versus 71.73 for 6pt+P3P; v3 Table 3 reports Cambridge values of 33.18 versus 38.44 for the corresponding solver families. These different settings do not establish a same-setting performance decline. v3 also adds +R/+F results and revised oracle rankings. v2's two-view Table 6 survives unchanged as v3 Table 4.

M1.justification: v3 adds fourth-point hypothesis filtering (+F) and Levenberg–Marquardt refinement on the original four correspondences (+R), with calibrated and partially calibrated variants. These modify the solver procedure beyond v2's existing RANSAC local optimization. The underlying virtual-correspondence construction, neural architecture, and training loss remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, method motivation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Network details move into the supplement, the separate discussion is integrated into experiments, and supplementary sections are reorganized around mean-point analysis, learning, and validation. References move after the supplement, and the author list expands.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, and v3 adds multi-metric heatmaps, refinement plots, and extensive AUC-versus-runtime panels. Real-data tables are restructured around datasets and solver variants, while individual timings become standalone tables. Earlier mean-point heatmaps, network diagrams, and noise plots are relocated. v3 Tables 6 and 8 duplicate the alternative-metric results.

R1.justification: v3 adds existing 4p3vf homotopy solutions by Chien et al. and Dal Cin et al., materially changing the positioning from solving a previously unsolved problem to providing faster practical solutions. It also adds citations for SuperPoint, LightGlue, PoseLib, PointNet, and uncertainty propagation while trimming background references.

T1.justification: v3 Section 9.3 introduces a different mathematical definition of pose error: the maximum of rotation and translation errors across all three camera pairs. This supplements the retained metric based on averages for pairs 1–2 and 1–3. Lemma 1, its geometric proof, and the Sampson-loss expression are retained; configuration renotation is equivalent.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens practical validation through broader scene testing in two RANSAC frameworks, held-out parameter selection, refinement ablations, measured speed–accuracy trade-offs, and evaluation of all three camera pairs. It also clarifies failure conditions and qualifies the learning contribution. Removing KITTI and some real-data baselines reduces coverage, and the inconsistent oracle statements remain a reporting weakness, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same virtual-correspondence framework for three-camera relative pose estimation. All 19 pages of v2 and 22 pages of v3, including supplementary text, equations, figures, and tables, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original pose-estimation results on PhotoTourism and Cambridge Landmarks, alongside synthetic experiments, ablations, and supplementary comparisons.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic and real-data experiments, including PhotoTourism and KITTI comparisons, noise and outlier analyses, and supplementary two-view results.

C1.justification: V3 claims contributions covering calibrated and partially calibrated cameras, virtual correspondences, and preliminary learned prediction. V4 redefines the contribution around two calibrated-camera solver families and their practical integration into RANSAC. Its abstract explicitly conditions state-of-the-art performance on local optimization and introduces the claim that mean-point solvers are more robust and accurate than affine solvers.

C2.justification: V3 discusses small-overlap instability and proposes uncertainty propagation or better learned correspondences. V4 replaces that discussion with explanations of error propagation, ENM, and differing local-optimization behavior in PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, and claims scene dependence becomes negligible after ENM. It also discusses ENM's applicability limits and explicitly qualifies the two-view solvers as not outperforming the five-point solver.

D1.justification: V4 changes code access from a future availability promise to a repository link stated to be available. It specifies ENM's SVD/QR construction, GC-RANSAC's PROSAC sampling and DLSPnP refitting, stopping/threshold details, and HC loading overhead. V3's extensive network architecture, normalization, optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size, and training-data documentation is removed with the learned branch.

E1.justification: V4 adds evaluation on Aachen Day-Night v1.1 and controlled scenarios varying camera angles, camera distances, scene depths, and noise distributions. It removes evaluation of the shared-unknown-focal-length task. PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, ETH3D noise experiments, and two-view pose estimation already occur in v3 and are retained.

E2.justification: Alongside retained HC and 5pt+P3P baselines, v4 Table 2 evaluates 5pt+P3P with ENM, with refinement/filtering, and with both. The 6pt+P3P baseline and joint 5PC noise comparator disappear with their corresponding comparisons. Virtual-correspondence oracle controls are removed; the Nistér–Schaffalitzky oracle remains qualitatively evaluated in Section 8.6.

E3.justification: The selected shift changes from 0.04 to 0.08 times the longest triangle dimension. The ETH3D noise sweep expands from 0–4 to 0–16 pixels. Two-view RANSAC evaluation changes from GC-RANSAC in v3 Table 4 to a PoseLib iteration sweep in v4 Figure 10, and v4 introduces explicit 3/5/10-pixel threshold sweeps. These constitute substantial protocol revisions.

E4.justification: V4 adds controlled geometric sensitivity studies, Gaussian-versus-uniform noise tests, ENM ablations, and RANSAC-threshold sensitivity analyses. It revises the outlier study to Notre Dame at 40%, 60%, and 80% inliers, replacing earlier scenes and settings including 20% inliers. Most mean-point heatmaps remain, but v3's synthetic/Shop Facade heatmaps and quantitative oracle analyses are removed.

E5.justification: V3 Table 1 reports mean errors with accompanying ± values; v4's corresponding table drops these variability entries and reports medians and 20th percentiles. Boxplot quantiles and Gaussian fitting remain. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Main and supplementary results are extensively replaced or expanded. For example, PhotoTourism Table 2 reports AUC@10 of 70.47 for 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F in v3 and 76.87 in v4, with revised settings including δ; this is not an established same-setting gain. V4 adds affine, ENM, and Aachen results, while learned, shared-focal, and quantitative oracle result entries disappear.

M1.justification: V4 adds the affine-camera 4p3v(A) solver and early non-minimal refitting (ENM), which refits two-view geometry before triangulation and third-camera registration. It removes v3's learned-correspondence solvers and shared-unknown-focal-length solvers. The original mean-point construction, shifted variants, filtering, and four-point refinement remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. The method section shifts from calibrated/partially calibrated branches to approximate solvers and practical refinements. The supplement is reorganized around geometry, ablations, and real-data experiments, replacing its earlier mean-point/network/experiment organization. Author and affiliation text also changes.

P2.justification: V4 restructures Table 1 around four solvers with and without ENM and converts Table 2 into a full-width, three-dataset comparison. It adds geometric-sensitivity and threshold/ENM plots and removes the network diagram and partially calibrated displays. V3 Figures 2 and 6 are consolidated into v4 Figure 11, while selected retained heatmaps appear in the main text.

R1.justification: V4 substantially expands positioning around affine and para-perspective approximations, including new references to Horaud, Oberkampf, and weak-perspective projection, and a fuller discussion of the already-cited Pritts approach. It revises comparisons with epipole-search methods and removes neural-method references such as NeFSAC, PointNet, and Set Transformer. This exceeds bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: The epipolar-bound lemma and its proof are retained. V4 Section 6.2 adds a targeted algebraic derivation showing why the mean-point constraint is redundant for affine geometry but supplies an independent constraint for perspective geometry. V3's general minimal-configuration counting equation is removed. These are limited theoretical changes rather than a replacement of the central proof.

improvement.justification: V3 documents scene-dependent behavior but largely leaves individual geometric factors untested. V4 directly studies those factors and threshold sensitivity, explains and ablates ENM, and evaluates strengthened 5pt+P3P baselines, substantially improving validation of the calibrated-camera contribution. The constraint derivation and stated code availability further improve understanding and reproducibility. Removing partially calibrated and learned extensions and quantitative oracle controls reduces breadth and diagnostic evidence, but the stronger validation and practical guidance provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same three-camera relative-pose work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplements support reliable comparison despite substantial changes in title, scope, and organization.

after.justification: V4 reports original synthetic geometry experiments, ablations, and real-scene PoseLib and GC-RANSAC evaluations in Section 4 and supplementary Sections 6–8.

before.justification: V3 reports original real-scene evaluations, synthetic noise and outlier experiments, learned-correspondence results, and runtime measurements in Section 4 and the supplement.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion refocus the contribution from general additional drop-based regularization through AugSub to enabling strong masking through MaskSub. D1.justification: Appendix B adds HuggingFace and OpenCLIP implementation references, token-masking instructions, and CLIP hardware, batch-size and sample-budget details. Existing recipe tables and the main code link remain. v2 removes explicit dropout insertion locations and the parameter/FLOP columns from architecture comparison tables.

E1.justification: v2 adds eight GLUE tasks with BERT and CLIP pretraining on CC3M, CC12M and RedCaps, followed by zero-shot ImageNet evaluation. These extend coverage to language and multimodal learning. CLIP image-classification finetuning already existed in v1; the original vision datasets and downstream evaluations remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include BERT-base/large with 15% token masking and CLIP ViT-B/32 training with batch size 1,024, 128M seen samples and zero-shot evaluation. Table 8 introduces augmentation comparisons with GradAug trained for 200 epochs versus 400 for other methods. Existing image-classification recipe settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.5 tests removing the KD loss, expands masking-ratio sensitivity to include 0%, 40% and 60%, and introduces a supervised/KD loss-weight sweep. These directly examine components and hyperparameters beyond v1's analyses. Existing convergence, gradient, regularization and robustness analyses are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report three independent runs with different seeds and identical mean/standard-deviation results for regularization, method variants and transfer learning. v1 Tables A.1–A.4 correspond to v2 Tables A.9–A.12. E6.justification: Matched original benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial comparator, ablation and domain results. Examples include BERT-base GLUE averages of 80.9 without versus 81.6 with MaskSub, and CLIP zero-shot accuracies of 33.5 for baseline, 29.8 for masking and 37.6 for MaskSub. Table 10 adds an incorrect Cars gain of +1.3; 92.2 minus 80.9 equals 11.3.

M1.justification: The original classification procedure, shared network and averaged supervised/self-distillation losses remain unchanged under renaming. Appendix B adds a CLIP adaptation that distills the main model's image-text similarity matrix into a sub-model receiving masked images, extending the procedure beyond classifier-output distillation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around masking. Analysis and variant subsections change order, experiments are reorganized, and the appendix gains thematic subsections. R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against self-supervised pretraining, CLIP-based training and self-distillation, adding works such as GradAug, MixSKD, BERT and GLUE.
